When common porcelain operations that create objects are run, they will check whether the repository has grown substantially since the last maintenance, and if so run git gc automatically. See gc.auto below for how to disable this behavior.

Running git gc manually should only be needed when adding objects to a repository without regularly running such porcelain commands, to do a one-off repository optimization, or e.g. to clean up a suboptimal mass-import. --aggressive: Usually git gc runs very quickly while providing good disk space utilization and performance. This option will cause git gc to more aggressively optimize the repository at the expense of taking much more time. The effects of this optimization are mostly persistent. See the "AGGRESSIVE" section below for details.

When the --aggressive option is supplied, git-repack[1] will be invoked with the -f flag, which in turn will pass --no-reuse-delta to git-pack-objects[1]. This will throw away any existing deltas and re-compute them, at the expense of spending much more time on the repacking.

It’s probably not worth it to use this option on a given repository without running tailored performance benchmarks on it. It takes a lot more time, and the resulting space/delta optimization may or may not be worth it. Not using this at all is the right trade-off for most users and their repositories.

git gc tries very hard not to delete objects that are referenced anywhere in your repository. In particular, it will keep not only objects referenced by your current set of branches and tags, but also objects referenced by the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs (which may reference commits in branches that were later amended or rewound), and anything else in the refs/* namespace. Note that a note (of the kind created by git notes) attached to an object does not contribute in keeping the object alive. If you are expecting some objects to be deleted and they aren’t, check all of those locations and decide whether it makes sense in your case to remove those references.
However, these features fall short of a complete solution, so users who run commands concurrently have to live with some risk of corruption (which seems to be low in practice).

generated_answer: Git's porcelain commands that create new objects periodically check whether the repository has grown substantially since the last maintenance, and if so they invoke `git gc --auto` behind the scenes. The automatic run is triggered by two thresholds: `gc.auto` (default roughly 6700 loose objects, past which loose objects get packed) and `gc.autoPackLimit` (default 50 packs not marked with a `*.keep` file, past which packs get consolidated into one larger pack), and setting `gc.auto` to 0 disables the whole mechanism, as does setting `gc.autoPackLimit` to 0 for the pack-consolidation part. Because `gc.autoDetach` defaults to true, the auto run returns immediately and continues in the background on systems that support it, acting as a fallback when `maintenance.autoDetach` isn't set. When gc actually runs, it prunes unreachable loose objects older than a grace period—by default `prune --expire 2.weeks.ago`, plus `repack --cruft --cruft-expiration 2.weeks.ago` if cruft packs are enabled—which you can override with `gc.pruneExpire` using "now" to prune immediately or "never" to suppress pruning entirely. It is deliberately conservative about deletion, keeping anything referenced by branches, tags, the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs, and anything else under `refs/*`, though note that a `git notes` annotation does not keep its object alive, and reflog entries themselves eventually expire (90 days by default, 30 days for entries unreachable from the current tip). The main risk is running gc concurrently with another process writing to the repository: gc may delete an object that process created but hasn't yet referenced, which can make that process fail or even corrupt the repository if it later adds a reference to the deleted object. context_passages: A "shared cache" is a cache that stores responses for reuse by more than one user; shared caches are usually (but not always) deployed as a part of an intermediary. A "private cache", in contrast, is dedicated to a single user; often, they are deployed as a component of a user agent.¶

The primary mechanism for determining freshness is for an origin server to provide an explicit expiration time in the future, using either the Expires header field (Section 5.3) or the max-age response directive (Section 5.2.2.1). Generally, origin servers will assign future explicit expiration times to responses in the belief that the representation is not likely to change in a semantically significant way before the expiration time is reached.¶

Since origin servers do not always provide explicit expiration times, a cache MAY assign a heuristic expiration time when an explicit time is not specified, employing algorithms that use other field values (such as the Last-Modified time) to estimate a plausible expiration time. This specification does not provide specific algorithms, but it does impose worst-case constraints on their results.¶

A cache MUST NOT use heuristics to determine freshness when an explicit expiration time is present in the stored response. Because of the requirements in Section 3, heuristics can only be used on responses without explicit freshness whose status codes are defined as "heuristically cacheable" (e.g., see Section 15.1 of [HTTP]) and on responses without explicit freshness that have been marked as explicitly cacheable (e.g., with a public response directive).¶

If the response has a Last-Modified header field (Section 8.8.2 of [HTTP]), caches are encouraged to use a heuristic expiration value that is no more than some fraction of the interval since that time. A typical setting of this fraction might be 10%.¶

The Age header field is used to convey an estimated age of the response message when obtained from a cache. The Age field value is the cache's estimate of the number of seconds since the origin server generated or validated the response. The Age value is therefore the sum of the time that the response has been resident in each of the caches along the path from the origin server, plus the time it has been in transit along network paths.¶

The max-age request directive indicates that the client prefers a response whose age is less than or equal to the specified number of seconds. Unless the max-stale request directive is also present, the client does not wish to receive a stale response.¶

The max-stale request directive indicates that the client will accept a response that has exceeded its freshness lifetime. If a value is present, then the client is willing to accept a response that has exceeded its freshness lifetime by no more than the specified number of seconds. If no value is assigned to max-stale, then the client will accept a stale response of any age.¶

The proxy-revalidate response directive indicates that once the response has become stale, a shared cache MUST NOT reuse that response to satisfy another request until it has been successfully validated by the origin, as defined by Section 4.3. This is analogous to must-revalidate (Section 5.2.2.2), except that proxy-revalidate does not apply to private caches.¶

The s-maxage response directive indicates that, for a shared cache, the maximum age specified by this directive overrides the maximum age specified by either the max-age directive or the Expires header field.¶

In particular, the URI(s) in the Location and Content-Location response header fields (if present) are candidates for invalidation; other URIs might be discovered through mechanisms not specified in this document. However, a cache MUST NOT trigger an invalidation under these conditions if the origin (Section 4.3.1 of [HTTP]) of the URI to be invalidated differs from that of the target URI (Section 7.1 of [HTTP]). The no-store request directive indicates that a cache MUST NOT store any part of either this request or any response to it. This directive applies to both private and shared caches. "MUST NOT store" in this context means that the cache MUST NOT intentionally store the information in non-volatile storage and MUST make a best-effort attempt to remove the information from volatile storage as promptly as possible after forwarding it.¶

The must-revalidate directive is necessary to support reliable operation for certain protocol features. In all circumstances, a cache MUST NOT ignore the must-revalidate directive; in particular, if a cache is disconnected, the cache MUST generate an error response rather than reuse the stale response. The generated status code SHOULD be 504 (Gateway Timeout) unless another error status code is more applicable.¶

The unqualified private response directive indicates that a shared cache MUST NOT store the response (i.e., the response is intended for a single user). question: What do no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private and s-maxage mean for HTTP caches, and how is freshness determined?
context_passages: The primary mechanism for determining freshness is for an origin server to provide an explicit expiration time in the future, using either the Expires header field (Section 5.3) or the max-age response directive (Section 5.2.2.1). Generally, origin servers will assign future explicit expiration times to responses in the belief that the representation is not likely to change in a semantically significant way before the expiration time is reached.¶

Since origin servers do not always provide explicit expiration times, a cache MAY assign a heuristic expiration time when an explicit time is not specified, employing algorithms that use other field values (such as the Last-Modified time) to estimate a plausible expiration time. This specification does not provide specific algorithms, but it does impose worst-case constraints on their results.¶

A cache MUST NOT use heuristics to determine freshness when an explicit expiration time is present in the stored response. Because of the requirements in Section 3, heuristics can only be used on responses without explicit freshness whose status codes are defined as "heuristically cacheable" (e.g., see Section 15.1 of [HTTP]) and on responses without explicit freshness that have been marked as explicitly cacheable (e.g., with a public response directive).¶

If the response has a Last-Modified header field (Section 8.8.2 of [HTTP]), caches are encouraged to use a heuristic expiration value that is no more than some fraction of the interval since that time. A typical setting of this fraction might be 10%.¶

The max-age request directive indicates that the client prefers a response whose age is less than or equal to the specified number of seconds. Unless the max-stale request directive is also present, the client does not wish to receive a stale response.¶
The no-cache request directive indicates that the client prefers a stored response not be used to satisfy the request without successful validation on the origin server.¶

The must-revalidate response directive indicates that once the response has become stale, a cache MUST NOT reuse that response to satisfy another request until it has been successfully validated by the origin, as defined by Section 4.3.¶

The must-revalidate directive is necessary to support reliable operation for certain protocol features. In all circumstances, a cache MUST NOT ignore the must-revalidate directive; in particular, if a cache is disconnected, the cache MUST generate an error response rather than reuse the stale response. The generated status code SHOULD be 504 (Gateway Timeout) unless another error status code is more applicable.¶

The no-cache response directive, in its unqualified form (without an argument), indicates that the response MUST NOT be used to satisfy any other request without forwarding it for validation and receiving a successful response; see Section 4.3.¶
The no-store response directive indicates that a cache MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response and MUST NOT use the response to satisfy any other request.¶

The unqualified private response directive indicates that a shared cache MUST NOT store the response (i.e., the response is intended for a single user). It also indicates that a private cache MAY store the response, subject to the constraints defined in Section 3, even if the response would not otherwise be heuristically cacheable by a private cache.¶

The s-maxage response directive indicates that, for a shared cache, the maximum age specified by this directive overrides the maximum age specified by either the max-age directive or the Expires header field.¶
generated_answer: Freshness in HTTP caching is primarily determined by explicit expiration times that the origin server assigns using the Expires header or the max-age response directive, reflecting the server's belief that the representation will not change in a semantically significant way before that time. When no explicit expiration is present, a cache may apply a heuristic to estimate a plausible expiration time, but it must not use heuristics when an explicit time exists, and heuristics are only allowed for status codes defined as heuristically cacheable or responses explicitly marked cacheable (for example, with the public directive); a common heuristic uses the Last-Modified time, with the expiration set to no more than a fraction of the interval since that time, typically 10%. The unqualified no-cache response directive means the response must not be used to satisfy any other request without first forwarding it to the origin for validation and receiving a successful response, while the no-cache request directive similarly signals that the client prefers a stored response not be used without successful validation. The no-store directive is stricter, requiring that a cache not store any part of either the request or the response and not use the response to satisfy any other request at all. The must-revalidate response directive requires that once a response becomes stale, a cache must not reuse it until it has been successfully revalidated by the origin, and a cache must never ignore this directive—even when disconnected, it must generate an error response, typically 504 (Gateway Timeout), rather than serve the stale response. The unqualified private directive indicates the response is intended for a single user, so a shared cache must not store it, although a private (browser) cache may store it even if it would not otherwise be heuristically cacheable. Finally, s-maxage applies specifically to shared caches, specifying a maximum age that overrides whatever freshness lifetime was indicated by max-age or the Expires header. Together, these directives give origin servers and clients fine-grained control over whether responses are stored, when they must be revalidated, and how long different classes of cache may consider them fresh.
